chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Zurarah, who said:

I said: My garment was affected by blood from a nosebleed or some semen, and I marked its trace until I could get water for it. Then I got it, but the time of salat (prayer) came, and I forgot that there was something on my garment, so I prayed. Then afterward I remembered. He said: You repeat the salat (prayer) and wash it.

I said: What if I had not seen its place, but I knew that it had affected it, so I searched for it but could not find it, then when I had prayed I found it? He said: You wash it and repeat the salat (prayer).

I said: What if I thought that it had affected it, but I was not certain of that, so I looked and saw nothing, then I prayed, and afterward I saw something on it? He said: You wash it and do not repeat the salat (prayer). I said: Why is that? He said: Because you were upon certainty regarding your taharah (ritual purity), then you doubted, so it is not appropriate for you ever to overturn certainty with doubt.

I said: Suppose I know that it has affected it, but I do not know where it is so that I may wash it? He said: You wash the area of your garment which you think it has affected until you are certain of its taharah (ritual purity).
I said: Is it incumbent upon me, if I doubt whether something affected it, to inspect it? He said: No. Rather, you only want to remove the doubt that has occurred within yourself.

I said: What if I see it on my garment while I am in salat (prayer)? He said: You break the salat (prayer) and repeat it if you had doubted a place on it and then saw it. But if you had not doubted, then you saw it fresh, you cut off the prayer, wash it, then continue upon the salat (prayer), because you do not know—perhaps it is something that fell upon you. So it is not appropriate to overturn certainty with doubt.

key_terms.النَّاحِيَةَ: the side or area of the garment

ai.seo_question: If I discover najasah on my clothing after salat (prayer), do I have to repeat the prayer?
ai.summary: This hadith sets out legal rulings concerning najasah on one's garment during salat (prayer), distinguishing between certain knowledge, prior doubt, and later discovery. It is also a foundational text for the jurisprudential principle that certainty is not overturned by doubt.
